idiom_name: typed factory (overrides: Partial<User> = {}) => User with spread overrides
implementation_notes: TypeScript supplies the type-level half of the pattern: type the factory as (overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User => ({ ...defaults, ...overrides }) so a test may override only the fields it asserts and the compiler rejects unknown or mistyped ones, and mark the defaults with satisfies User so adding a field to the interface fails at the definition site instead of silently producing incomplete test data. For nested graphs a shallow Partial only relaxes the first level - thread a DeepPartial or a nested factory - and read-only types (Readonly<User>, Object.freeze) keep the default instance from being edited. The library form is fishery, whose Factory.define<User> types both defaults and per-call overrides; hand-written chained builders are for step-wise conditional construction only.
pitfalls: Partial<User> only relaxes the top level: nested required members stay required, so deep overrides need a DeepPartial or a nested factory rather than a cast.
A factory whose defaults are annotated merely as User can drift from the interface without a compile error when a field is added - use satisfies at the definition site so drift is caught.
Spreading an overrides object typed with optional properties can leave required fields undefined at run time; strip undefined entries before spreading.
